summary: This unit teaches you to give a full manicure and pedicure with a hand, arm, foot and lower-leg massage: analyse the nails and skin, spot conditions that stop or restrict the service, keep the station and foot spa hygienic, care for the cuticles, remove hard skin safely, apply polish including a French finish, and adapt the service for different clients. You will also learn the structure of the nail, work safely with chemicals and electrical equipment, and give aftercare advice and rebooking.

blocks.p: This unit takes you from the basic manicure and pedicure to a full, professional service. You will analyse the client's nails and skin before you begin, understand how the nail is built and grows, keep to a strict hygiene routine, give a longer massage, adapt the service for the client in front of you, and advise her on how to look after her hands and feet at home.
It is for COSMETOLOGY LEVEL 2 trainees. Clients pay for time and care as well as for the polish, so your consultation, your gentleness and your clean-up count as much as the finished nails.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and two group practical tasks, a full manicure with a hand and arm massage and a full pedicure with a foot and lower-leg massage. You work in pairs as therapist and client, and each member also takes a job for the group, such as setting up, taking photos or checking the cleaning log. A partner with a contraindication is not treated; the assessor gives you a model instead.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In practical work, photograph the hands, feet and work area only, never the client's face.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: The nail, nail growth and common conditions

blocks.p: The nail is made of **keratin**, the same hard protein as hair. It protects the tips of the fingers and toes. To work safely you must know which parts are hard and dead, which are living, and which must never be cut or pressed.

head: Part
What it is
Why it matters to you
rows: Nail plate
The hard, see-through part of the nail that we paint. It is made of dead keratin and has no feeling.
File and polish it. It must be clean and oil-free for polish to stick.
Nail bed
The skin under the nail plate that holds it in place and gives it its pink colour. It is living.
Do not file or push deep into it.
Matrix
The living part under the skin at the base of the nail. It makes new nail cells. The pale half-moon you can see is the **lunula**.
Pressing on it, or hitting it, can damage the new nail: ridges, white spots or a split.
Cuticle
A thin layer of dead skin that sticks to the nail plate near its base.
Softened and gently pushed back; only loose dead skin is trimmed.
Eponychium
The living fold of skin at the base of the nail, from which the cuticle grows.
Do not cut it: infection can enter.
Free edge
The part of the nail plate that grows past the end of the finger or toe.
The part you shape.
Hyponychium
The skin under the free edge, where the nail plate and the fingertip meet. It forms a seal that keeps germs out.
Do not dig under the free edge with a sharp tool.
Nail walls and grooves
The folds of skin at the sides of the nail and the channels the nail grows along.
Digging into the grooves causes ingrown nails and infection.

ul: Fingernails grow about **3 mm a month** on average, so a nail takes roughly four to six months to grow from base to tip. **Toenails grow more slowly** than fingernails and take a year or more.
Growth is faster in summer, in young people, in pregnancy and on the hand you use most. It is slower in cold weather, in older people and in poor health.
Healthy nails are smooth, pinkish and slightly flexible, with a curved surface and an even colour.

head: Condition
What you see
What it means for the service
rows: Leuconychia
Small white spots on the nail plate.
Usually from a knock to the matrix; harmless and grows out. **Not a contraindication**: the service goes ahead.
Ridges (vertical)
Fine lines running from base to tip.
Common, increasing with age. Buff lightly; use a ridge-filling base coat if the client wants.
Beau's lines
Grooves running across the nail, often after an illness, a fever or a shock to the body.
They grow out with the nail. Not a reason to refuse the service. Mention it if she asks, and suggest she mentions it to her doctor if there are several.
Onycholysis
The nail lifting away from the nail bed, with a white or yellow area under it.
Do not push or file under the lifted part. Keep it dry and clean. If it is painful, discoloured or spreading, refer: it may be an infection.
Fungal infection (onychomycosis)
Thick, yellow, brown or white, crumbly nails; may lift.
**Contraindication.** Do not treat; refer to a doctor. It spreads on files, clippers and foot-spa water.
Paronychia
Red, swollen, painful skin around the nail, sometimes with pus.
**Contraindication.** A bacterial infection; do not treat, refer.
Bruised nail
A dark red, purple or black patch under the nail after a knock.
Avoid pressure on it. If painful or you do not know the cause, advise a doctor. Do not drill or pierce.
Split or brittle nails
Layers peeling at the free edge.
File gently in one direction, do not saw; moisturise; advise gloves.
Bitten nails
Short, ragged nails and sore cuticles.
Not a contraindication unless the skin is broken. Give a gentle manicure and advise on home care.
Hangnail
A small strip of torn skin at the side of a nail.
Trim only the torn piece, with clean nippers.
Ingrown nail
The edge of the nail growing into the skin; red and sore.
Refer to a podiatrist or doctor. Avoid the area.
Corns and calluses
Hard, thick patches on feet, from pressure or rubbing. A corn is smaller, with a hard core.
Gently smooth a callus with a file. A painful or bleeding corn is referred; do not cut it.

blocks.p: A **podiatrist** is a foot specialist who treats ingrown nails, corns, verrucae and other foot problems. Know where one is near you, so you can give the client a name.
The consultation tells you what the client wants and whether it is safe to give it. Greet her, seat her comfortably, explain the service, and listen.

flow: Greet the client and explain the service
Ask about health, medicines, allergies, job, hobbies and home care
Ask what she wants from the service
Wash your hands
Look at the hands or feet and the nails in good light
Check the skin and nails (analysis)
Decide: go ahead, adapt, or refer
Suggest the treatment, shape, products and price in J$
Agree and write it on the record card
Ask the client to sign it

head: Ask about
Why
rows: Health: diabetes, circulation problems, arthritis, recent injuries, pregnancy
Some conditions need care or a doctor's advice. Heat and pressure may need to change.
Allergies to nail products, latex gloves, fragrance or metals
So you avoid the product or choose another glove.
Job, hobbies and sport
Water, chemicals and manual work wear nails down. This decides the shape, length and colour she can wear.
Home care and habits
Biting, picking, using nails as tools, and how often she washes up or cleans.
What she wants
Shape, length, colour, finish and the time she has.

ul: **Skin:** dry or oily, hard skin, cuts, redness, swelling, signs of infection (athlete's foot, warts), scars.
**Nails:** shape, length, strength, ridges, white spots, splitting, lifting, bruising, discolouration or signs of fungus.
Look, then **feel** gently: warmth, swelling or pain tell you something that the eye does not.
Look at the feet **between the toes**.

blocks.h: What stops the service, what restricts it

head: Stops the service on that area: refer
Why
rows: Fungal infections: athlete's foot, fungal nails
Contagious; spread on tools, towels and spa water. Refer to a doctor or pharmacist.
Bacterial infections: paronychia, boils, infected cuts
Contagious; massage and tools spread them. Refer to a doctor.
Viral infections: warts and verrucae
Contagious. Refer.
Broken or bleeding skin; open cuts
Germs enter, and products sting.
Severe nail lifting or damage
Needs medical advice.
Swelling, a recent fracture or sprain
Massage and pressure could harm.
Inflamed or weeping skin conditions
Broken skin and pain.
Ingrown toenail that is red or sore
Refer to a podiatrist.

head: Restricts the service: adapt
How
rows: A small cut or bruise
Avoid the area; cover it with a plaster if it is a cut and the Centre allows.
Varicose veins
Do not massage over the veins; massage only clear areas, or leave out the lower-leg massage.
Diabetes or poor circulation
Ask for the doctor's advice; use warm, not hot, water; file instead of cutting where possible; do not cut cuticles; light pressure; check the feet carefully.
Arthritis or painful joints
Very light massage, or leave it out if her doctor advises; support the hand; short sessions.
Dry, sensitive skin; mild eczema that is unbroken
Mild, fragrance-free products; warm water.
Allergy to a product
Use a different one, or leave that step out.

blocks.note: You are not a doctor. Never tell a client she has a disease. Say kindly, and in private, what you have seen and why you cannot treat the area today. Suggest a doctor, a pharmacist or a podiatrist, and write it on her record card. A client who is partnered with a trainee in practical work and has a contraindication is not treated; her partner works on a model instead.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: A client with diabetes may have reduced feeling and slow healing in her feet. She may not feel water that is too hot, too much pressure, or a small cut, and an injury can become a serious infection. Ask about diabetes in the consultation, record it, and follow the adaptations above.

sections.title: Hygiene, tools and the foot spa

blocks.p: Nail services pass infection from client to client unless every tool, towel and bowl is clean. The routine below is not optional. It protects your clients, you and the Centre.

head: Word
What it means
Used for
rows: Cleaning
Removing skin, dust and product with soap and water and a brush. Always first.
All tools and surfaces before disinfecting.
Disinfecting
Using a salon disinfectant, mixed and timed as the maker says, to kill most germs on a cleaned tool.
Metal tools, bowls, the foot spa, surfaces.
Sterilising
Killing all germs, including spores, in an **autoclave** (steam under pressure).
Metal tools, where the Centre has an autoclave.
UV cabinet
A cabinet that **stores** tools already clean and disinfected.
Storage only. It does not disinfect dirty tools.

flow: Put on gloves
Wash the tool with soap, water and a brush to remove skin and dust
Rinse and dry
Immerse it fully in salon disinfectant for the maker's time, or sterilise it in the autoclave
Rinse if the maker says; dry
Store it in a clean, covered container or a clean UV cabinet
Wash your hands

ul: Single-use items are used once and thrown away: **emery boards and buffers, orange sticks, cotton, toe separators, wooden spatulas**, and pumice where the Centre says so. Porous items cannot be disinfected.
Any blade or sharp item goes into the sharps box.
A fresh towel for every client; used towels go into the laundry bin and are washed hot.

blocks.p: A warm, wet foot spa is the best place for germs to grow. Treat it as a tool that touches every client.

flow: Drain the water
Put on gloves
Scrub away debris and skin with a brush and detergent
For a whirlpool spa, run detergent and water through the jets as the maker says
Rinse
Disinfect for the contact time
Rinse and dry
Write it in the cleaning log: date, time, product and your initials

ul: **Check before every client** that the spa was cleaned and disinfected after the last one. If it was not, do it first.
Pedicure liners, where used, are single-use, but the spa is still cleaned.

A **cleaning log** is the written record that shows when the foot spa was cleaned and disinfected. It protects the Centre if there is a complaint and shows the instructor that the routine was followed.
Do not use a spa with a damaged cable or a leak. Label it and report it.
Wash your hands before and after every client. Dry on a clean towel or paper.
Wear **disposable gloves** when there is a risk of touching blood or broken skin, and when cleaning the spa. Nitrile or vinyl gloves suit people who are allergic to latex.
Clean hands, short nails, and no rings that trap dirt.
Cover your own cuts.

flow: Stop; tell the client
Put on gloves
Press clean cotton on the cut until the bleeding stops
Apply an antiseptic
Cover with a plaster if the client agrees
Put the cotton and gloves in a sealed bag
Clean and disinfect the tool and surface
Wash your hands
Record it

blocks.note: Cleaning logs, record cards and consent forms hold personal information. Keep them private, as Jamaica's data protection law expects.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: The client sits facing you with her forearm on a cushion or folded towel. You sit with a straight back and the work in good light.

flow: Set up; wash your hands; cleanse the client's hands
Consult; check; record
Remove old polish
File to the agreed shape with a fine file
Apply cuticle remover; soak the fingers in a finger bowl
Dry; push back the cuticles; nip hangnails only
Clean under the free edge; buff if needed
Repeat on the other hand
Hand and arm massage with cream
Remove oil from the nail plates
Base coat, two thin coats of colour, top coat, capped
Clean the skin; check; give aftercare

ul: Press a soaked pad on each nail for a moment, then **wipe from the base towards the tip**.

Use a **fine-grit** file on natural nails. The **grit number** tells you how coarse the file is: the higher the number, the finer the file. Coarse files (low numbers, such as 80 or 100) are for artificial nails; natural nails are filed with a fine grit (about 180 or 240), or the fine side of an emery board.
File from each side to the centre, in one direction. Sawing splits the layers of the nail.

The usual **shapes**: square, squoval, round, oval and pointed. For a client who does a lot of work with her hands, a **short square or squoval** shape is usually the strongest and most practical. An **oval** has a rounded tip like an egg and suits most fingers.

**Cuticle remover** (or softener) loosens dead skin on the nail plate around the cuticle. Apply it to the cuticle, **not the whole nail and not the skin**, and leave it for the time the maker gives. It is strong and can **irritate the skin** if it is left on, so wash it off after that time.
Soak the fingers in the **finger bowl** of warm, soapy water for a few minutes.
Dry the hand and push the cuticles back **gently, once softened**, with a metal or rubber pusher or a wrapped orange stick. The matrix lies under the cuticle: pushing hard damages it.
Use the nippers only for hangnails and loose dead skin.

blocks.p: A buffer smooths ridges and gives a natural shine. Use the coarse side lightly first, then the fine side. Buff in one direction and for a few seconds only: heavy buffing thins the nail and makes it hot.

head: Movement
How you do it
Effects
rows: Effleurage
A smooth, gliding stroke from the fingers up the arm towards the elbow.
Spreads the cream, warms the skin and relaxes the client. Used to begin, to link movements and to finish.
Petrissage
Kneading: lifting and squeezing the muscles of the forearm and the palm.
Improves blood flow and eases tight muscles.
Friction
Small, firm circles with the thumbs around the joints and across the back of the hand.
Loosens stiffness.
Tapotement
Light, quick tapping with the fingertips.
Stimulating. It is not normally used in a nail massage.

ul: Warm a little cream in your hands, and keep one hand in contact with the client throughout.
Keep an even rhythm and pressure, and ask if the pressure suits her.
You can gently move each finger joint through its normal range.

**Change or leave out** the massage over cuts, bruises, swelling, skin infections, recent injuries and very painful joints. For arthritis use very light pressure, or leave it out if her doctor advises.
Finish with effleurage; remove all cream and oil from the nail plates with remover.

blocks.h: Adapting for a client who does not want polish

blocks.p: Some clients, among them many men, want clean, healthy nails but no colour. Give the same manicure, then **buff to a natural shine** and finish with cuticle oil in place of polish.

ul: Do not scold. Give a gentle manicure: soften the cuticles, shape what is there and moisturise.
Do not nip at sore skin. Avoid long files and long artificial extensions on very short bitten nails.
Advise: cuticle oil, hand cream, a good-tasting nail strengthener, and keeping the hands busy. Suggest she comes back regularly: a good-looking set of nails is the best reason to stop biting.
If the skin is broken or infected, do not treat the area.

blocks.p: Seat the client comfortably with her feet raised and supported, her back supported and a towel under the feet. You sit with a straight back and the client's foot **raised on a rest** at a height you can reach without bending, to protect your own back.

flow: Check the foot spa was cleaned and disinfected; fill with warm water
Consult; check the feet, including between the toes; record
Wash your hands; gloves if needed
Cleanse the feet; remove old polish
Soak the feet for a few minutes
Dry one foot and cut the toenails straight across with toenail clippers
File the edges smooth
Cuticle remover; push back gently; nip loose skin only
Smooth hard skin on the heels and balls of the feet with a foot file or pumice
Foot scrub
Rinse and dry well, especially between the toes
Foot and lower-leg massage
Remove oil from the nail plates
Toe separators; base coat, two coats of colour, top coat
Open-toed slippers; aftercare; record
Clean and disinfect the spa; fill in the log

ul: **Toenail clippers** (not the small nail scissors or nippers) are best for toenails, which are thicker and flatter than fingernails.
Cut **straight across, level with the end of the toe**, in two or three small cuts. Do not round the corners down into the skin: this causes **ingrown toenails**. Do not cut too short.
Smooth the edges with a file, in one direction, and take the sharp point off the corners.
**The safest way** to smooth a callus is to use a **foot file or pumice stone, gently**, on softened skin, in one direction.
**Leave some hard skin.** It protects the foot from pressure and rubbing; taking it all away leaves tender skin that blisters.
**Never use a blade** or a cheese-grater type of tool in this service.
A foot scrub, a gritty cream that lifts dead skin, is massaged in circles over the feet and then rinsed. Use it only on unbroken skin.
A painful or bleeding corn, or a deep crack, is referred to a podiatrist or doctor.
**Dry the feet well, especially between the toes.** Damp skin there starts fungal infections such as athlete's foot.
The foot and lower-leg massage uses the same movements: effleurage from the toes up the leg, petrissage on the calf and sole, friction on the sole and ankle.
**Varicose veins:** do not massage over the veins. Massage only the clear areas, or leave the lower leg out.
Do not massage a swollen leg, a calf that is hot, red and painful (possible blood clot: the client must see a doctor), cuts or infected skin.

blocks.p: Remove the oil from the nail plates, place the **toe separators** to keep the toes apart while polish dries, and apply the coats as for the hands. The client wears open-toed disposable slippers until the polish is dry.

ul: Sit on a stool at the right height, with a straight back and the foot raised on a rest: this protects your back and neck.
Keep your elbows close to your body, and take short breaks between clients to stretch.
Good light: bend towards the work with your eyes, not your back.
After the massage the nail plates carry cream and oil. Wipe each one with remover so that the polish can stick: **oil stops polish sticking**.
Roll the bottle gently between your palms. Do not shake: it makes bubbles.

head: Coat
Purpose
How
rows: Base coat
Protects the nail from stains and helps the colour to stick.
One thin coat; cap the free edge.
Colour, first coat
Starts the colour.
About three strokes: centre, then each side; a tiny gap at the cuticle.
Colour, second coat
Evens out the colour.
After the first has dried a little; cap the free edge.
Top coat
Protects and adds shine.
Thin; cap the free edge.

ul: **Two thin coats** dry harder and are less likely to chip or bubble than one thick coat.
**Capping** (wrapping) the free edge means brushing polish across the very tip of the nail to seal it. It makes the polish last longer.
Wipe one side of the brush on the neck of the bottle so you do not flood the cuticle.
Tidy polish off the skin with a **fine brush or wrapped orange stick dipped in remover** before it dries.
Check for smudges, bubbles and bare patches, and let the polish harden before the client puts her hands or feet away.

flow: Apply base coat
Paint a curved white 'smile line' across the tip of each nail, following the natural curve of the free edge
Let it dry
Apply a sheer pink or nude colour over the whole nail
Apply top coat and cap the edge

blocks.p: A French finish needs a steady hand and even smile lines on all ten nails. If one is uneven, wipe it off with a wrapped orange stick and redo it. Tip guides (small stickers) can help beginners.

blocks.h: Products and when to use them

head: Product
Use
Note
rows: Cuticle remover or softener
Softens dead skin around the cuticle.
Time as the maker says; wash off.
Cuticle oil
Conditions the cuticle skin.
Daily at home; applied after polish has dried.
Hand cream
Moisturises the hands; massage medium.
Remove from the nail plate before polish.
Foot cream (rich)
Moisturises dry, rough feet at the end of a pedicure.
Not between the toes.
Foot scrub
Lifts dead skin.
Unbroken skin only.
Top coat refresher
A thin top coat added at home every few days.
Makes the polish last longer.
Sunscreen for the hands
Protects hands outdoors.
Used by clients who are outdoors a lot.

ul: Polish, remover and some other nail products are **flammable and give off fumes**: store them in labelled containers, lids closed, in a cool place, away from heat, flames and sunlight, and out of children's reach.
Keep the room **ventilated**. No smoking near them.
Keep only the amount you need at the station. Wipe up spills at once. Put used pads in a lined, covered bin.
Read the label and the **safety data sheet**; follow the maker's instructions.
Wear gloves when using disinfectants, and mix them only as the label says. Never mix two chemicals together.
If a product splashes in an eye, rinse with plenty of clean, cool water and get medical help.

head: Hazard
How you prevent it
rows: Water and electricity (foot spa, lamps, dryers)
Check the plug and cable for damage before use
Keep the socket and cable away from water; dry hands
Fill or empty the spa as the maker says
Faulty equipment: unplug, label, report
Water on the floor
Put towels down; wipe splashes at once
Help the client in and out of the chair
Fumes and fire
Ventilate; lids closed; no flames; products stored away from heat
Chemicals
Gloves; labels and safety data sheets; correct dilution
Cuts
Gloves; clean cotton and antiseptic; record
Your posture
Straight back; the client's foot raised on a rest; short breaks
Hot water
Test it with your inner wrist; warm, not hot; extra care for clients with diabetes

blocks.note: Jamaica's electricity supply is 110 V, or 220 V for some equipment, at 50 Hz. Check that the label on the foot spa matches the socket. The summer months are very hot: take care that the water is not heated beyond comfort, and offer the client water to drink.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Advice
Why
rows: Wear gloves for housework, washing and gardening; do not use the nails as tools.
Protects the nails, the polish and the skin.
Hand cream several times a day and cuticle oil each night.
Keeps skin and cuticles supple.
File a rough edge with a fine file, in one direction.
Stops tears.
A thin top coat every few days; sunscreen on the hands.
Makes polish last and protects the skin.
Wash and dry the feet daily, especially between the toes; clean socks; shoes that fit well.
Prevents fungal infection, corns and ingrown nails.
Foot cream on the heels, not between the toes.
Softens hard skin without making the toe spaces damp.
Cut toenails straight across; see a podiatrist for corns or ingrown nails.
Prevents and treats foot problems.
See a doctor for redness, swelling, pain or a nail that changes colour.
May be an infection.

ul: Suggest only products that meet her needs: cuticle oil, foot cream, a nail strengthener. Say how to use them.
Give the price in J$ and let her decide. No pressure.
A client usually returns for a manicure or pedicure **about every two to four weeks**. Suggest a date, book it if she agrees, and write it on her card.
Thank the client, and make sure she has her belongings and her slippers.

blocks.p: The record card is signed by the client. It lets the next therapist plan safely and shows what was done.

head: What to record
Example
rows: Date, client, signature
07/11/2026, Mrs Y. Francis, Black River (signed)
Health and allergies
No diabetes; allergic to latex gloves
Analysis
Nails strong, ridged; small cut on left index, avoided; no infection
Service
Full manicure; squoval; hand and arm massage
Products and colour
Cuticle remover, hand cream, base coat, pink polish, top coat
Reactions
None
Advice and rebooking
Gloves for housework; hand cream; rebook in 3 weeks
Therapist
S. Brown (trainee), checked by the instructor

ul: I can name the parts of the nail and say which are living and which are dead.
I can say how fast nails grow and how fingernails and toenails differ.
I can recognise leuconychia, ridges, Beau's lines, onycholysis and hangnails, and say what to do.
I can carry out a consultation and a nail and skin analysis.
I can name infections that stop the service and conditions that restrict it, and refer correctly to a doctor, pharmacist or podiatrist.
I can explain why a client with diabetes needs extra care and what I change.
I can clean, then disinfect or sterilise, metal tools, and say what a UV cabinet is for.
I can identify single-use items and handle sharps.
I can clean and disinfect the foot spa and fill in the cleaning log.
I can file nails with the correct grit and in the correct direction, and name the nail shapes.
I can use cuticle remover and push back cuticles safely.
I can give a hand and arm massage with effleurage, petrissage and friction, and say when to change it.
I can give a full pedicure, cutting toenails straight across and smoothing hard skin safely.
I can adapt the service for varicose veins, arthritis, bitten nails and a client who does not want polish.
I can apply base coat, two capped coats of colour and top coat, and a French finish.
I can work safely with electricity, water, chemicals and fumes, and sit correctly.
I can give aftercare and product advice in J$ and rebook, and complete a record card.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason for each step. For example: 'I cut toenails straight across, so that the corners do not grow into the skin.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: Nail plate
The hard, see-through part of the nail that is filed and painted.
Nail bed
The skin under the nail plate that holds it in place.
Matrix
The living part at the base of the nail where new nail cells are made.
Lunula
The pale half-moon at the base of the nail, the visible part of the matrix.
Cuticle
The dead skin that sticks to the nail plate near its base.
Eponychium
The living fold of skin at the base of the nail.
Free edge
The part of the nail plate that grows past the fingertip.
Hyponychium
The skin under the free edge that seals out germs.
Leuconychia
Small white spots on the nail plate; not a contraindication.
Beau's lines
Grooves across the nail, often after illness.
Onycholysis
The nail lifting away from the nail bed.
Paronychia
A bacterial infection of the skin around the nail.
Athlete's foot (tinea pedis)
A fungal infection of the skin, often between the toes.
Verruca
A wart on the foot, caused by a virus.
Hangnail
A small torn strip of skin at the side of a nail.
Callus
Thick, hard skin on the heels and balls of the feet.
Podiatrist
A foot specialist who treats ingrown nails, corns and other foot problems.
Contraindication
A reason a service must not be carried out or must be changed.
Autoclave
A machine that sterilises with steam under pressure.
UV cabinet
A cabinet for storing tools that are already clean and disinfected.
Single-use
Used on one client and thrown away.
Cleaning log
The written record of when the foot spa was cleaned and disinfected.
Grit
The coarseness of a nail file: the higher the number, the finer the file.
Finger bowl
The bowl of warm, soapy water for soaking the fingers.
Cuticle remover
A product that softens dead skin around the cuticle; washed off after its time.
Cuticle pusher
A tool of metal or rubber for pushing back softened cuticles.
Effleurage
Smooth, gliding strokes that begin and end a massage.
Petrissage
Kneading that lifts and presses the muscles.
Friction
Small, firm circles with the thumbs or fingertips.
Tapotement
Light, quick tapping with the fingertips.
Toe separators
Foam pieces that keep the toes apart while polish dries.
Capping
Brushing polish across the tip of the nail to seal it.
French finish
A white tip over a sheer pink or nude nail.
Record card
The client's signed record of her health, analysis, service, products and advice.

c1.title: A hairdresser's hands in Savanna-la-Mar
c1.text: Camille Hylton, 31, a hairdresser in Savanna-la-Mar, Westmoreland, comes for a manicure on her only free afternoon. Her hands are dry and her nails are splitting at the free edge from constant wet work and chemicals. She has a deep groove across both thumbnails that she says appeared after a bad bout of dengue fever three months ago. Trainee Roxanne checks the hands and finds no cuts or redness.

c2.title: A pedicure for a retired farmer in Christiana
c2.text: Mr Winston Reid, 70, a retired farmer in Christiana, Manchester, books a pedicure with his daughter. He has arthritis in his hands and diabetes, and his feet are tender. He has thick, dry calluses on both heels. On the left leg trainee Marlon sees swollen, twisted veins running down the calf. Mr Reid says he does not feel heat well in his feet.

c3.title: A busy Friday at a salon in Papine
c3.text: At a salon in Papine, St Andrew, trainee Shanice has four pedicures booked back to back on Friday afternoon. She has a foot spa with whirlpool jets. Between clients she drains the spa and gives it a quick rinse, then fills it again. The cleaning log on the wall has not been filled in since Monday. One client, Mrs Hall, notices and asks Shanice, 'Was this cleaned after the last lady?'

c4.title: Polish that chips in Black River
c4.text: Shelly-Ann has a manicure at a nail studio in Black River, St Elizabeth. The polish chips at the tips after two days. Trainee Amoy had massaged her hands with a rich cream, then applied the base coat directly over the nails. She put on one thick coat of colour and did not cap the free edge. She also used a coarse 100-grit file on Shelly-Ann's natural nails to shape them.

c5.title: A male client at a barber-and-nail shop in Ewarton
c5.text: Delroy Facey, 38, a mechanic, comes to a combined barber and nail shop in Ewarton, St Catherine, for a manicure. He bites his nails, and his cuticles are sore. He tells trainee Kayla he wants 'nothing shiny, just neat'. His hands have engine oil in the creases and a small dry cut on one knuckle.

questions.q: What do the grooves across Camille's thumbnails most likely show?
o: A fungal infection that spread from her work with chemicals
Beau's lines from the illness, which grow out with the nail
A habit of tapping the nails on hard surfaces during work
Damage from a coarse file used at her last manicure
questions.why: Grooves across the nail, which appear weeks after a fever or illness, are Beau's lines. They grow out as the nail grows and do not stop the service.

questions.q: Which advice for Camille's splitting nails is best?
o: File back and forth quickly and wear rubber gloves for wet work
File gently in one direction and wear gloves for wet work
Keep nails very long to allow room for the layers to heal
Soak the nails in hot water daily to make them stronger
questions.why: Sawing splits the layers, so nails are filed in one direction. Gloves keep water and chemicals off. Soaking in hot water dries the nail further, and long nails catch and tear.

questions.q: Where on the nail should Roxanne put the cuticle remover?
o: On the cuticle area at the base of each nail
Over the whole nail plate, to soften the nail
Along the free edge, to loosen dirt under it
Over the skin of the whole finger, for an even soak
questions.why: The remover loosens dead skin at the cuticle, so it goes there only, for the maker's time, and is then washed off. On living skin or the nail plate it does no good and can irritate.

questions.q: After the massage, what must Roxanne do before the base coat?
o: Put on a second layer of hand cream to protect the nail
Press the cream into the nail plate so it can soak in
Wipe the oil and cream off every nail plate with remover
File the surface of each nail with the coarse side of a buffer
questions.why: Oil and cream on the nail plate stop polish from sticking, and the polish will lift or peel. Each nail is wiped with remover before the base coat is applied.

questions.q: What should Marlon do about the veins on Mr Reid's left calf during the massage?
o: Massage firmly over the veins to move the blood along
Leave the lower-leg massage out of the left leg altogether
Use light effleurage over the veins and heavy petrissage elsewhere
Avoid the veins, massage only clear areas and use light pressure
questions.why: Massage over swollen, twisted (varicose) veins can damage them, so they are avoided. The clear areas can still be massaged, with comfortable pressure.

questions.q: How should Marlon prepare the foot spa water for Mr Reid?
o: Fill it hot and let it cool for a minute before his feet go in
Use warm water, tested with his own wrist, and keep the soak short
Use the same temperature as for other clients, since he has asked for it
Ask Mr Reid to test it with his foot and tell him when it is warm enough
questions.why: A client with diabetes may not feel heat in the feet, so the therapist tests the water carefully, keeps it warm and not hot, and keeps the soak short. Mr Reid cannot be relied on to judge the temperature himself.

questions.q: Which is the safest way to deal with Mr Reid's thick heel calluses?
o: Remove all the hard skin with a blade for a smooth finish
Leave the calluses alone, since touching them could cause an infection
Smooth them gently with a foot file, leaving some hard skin
Soak the heels for twenty minutes and scrub them with a coarse brush
questions.why: A callus is smoothed gently with a foot file or pumice, leaving some hard skin to protect the foot. A blade can cut a client with diabetes, and long soaks and hard scrubbing damage the skin.

questions.q: Because of Mr Reid's arthritis, how should Marlon change the hand massage?
o: Give a longer massage so that the joints are loosened fully
Use very light pressure and support the hand, or leave it out
Bend each finger firmly to make the joints move as far as they go
Replace it with tapotement over the knuckles to stimulate them
questions.why: Painful joints are handled gently: light pressure, a supported hand and a short session, or no massage if his doctor advises. Firm bending and tapping can hurt and inflame the joints.

questions.q: What should Shanice have done between clients?
o: Drained, scrubbed, flushed the jets, disinfected and logged it
Added disinfectant to the old water and left it for a few minutes
Drained the spa, rinsed it and wiped it dry with a clean towel
Drained the spa and used a fresh liner, since the liner protects the spa
questions.why: A whirlpool spa and its jets harbour germs in warm water. After each client it is drained, scrubbed, cleaned through the jets, disinfected for the maker's time, rinsed and written in the cleaning log.

questions.q: Why does the empty cleaning log matter?
o: It is needed only if the instructor asks to see it
It shows how many clients were served on each day
It is the only way the Centre can tell how much disinfectant is used
It is the record that proves the spa was cleaned and disinfected
questions.why: The log shows when and how the spa was cleaned, so that the Centre can show the routine was followed and check it if a client complains of an infection. A blank log gives no proof.

questions.q: Mrs Hall asks whether the spa was cleaned. What should Shanice do?
o: Tell her it was cleaned, as it was drained and rinsed
Say that the spa is cleaned every Monday morning
Clean and disinfect the spa properly now, then tell her
Fill the spa and ask her to tell the manager if she is unhappy
questions.why: A client who asks is entitled to a straight answer and a safe service. Shanice cleans and disinfects the spa before she goes on, and says so. Saying it was cleaned when it was only rinsed is not honest.

questions.q: Why is a whirlpool spa a bigger infection risk than a plain bowl that is emptied after each client?
o: Warm water left in its jets and pipes lets germs breed
The jets make the water too hot for most clients to bear
The jets scrape the skin of the feet and open small cuts
The spa uses more electricity than a plain bowl does
questions.why: Water and skin debris stay in the jets and pipes, where warm, damp conditions let bacteria and fungi grow, and the next client's feet then soak in them. That is why the jets are flushed with detergent and disinfected as the maker says, and the cleaning is logged.

questions.q: Which mistake in Shelly-Ann's manicure was most likely to cause chipping at the tips?
o: Using a thick base coat that stayed soft under the colour
Shaping the nails with a fine-grit file, which left the edge too smooth
Not capping the free edge, and one thick coat of colour
Applying the top coat before the colour had dried a little
questions.why: A thick coat dries soft on the surface and chips, and an uncapped free edge leaves the tip unprotected. Thin, capped coats last longer.

questions.q: Why was the base coat applied directly after the cream a problem?
o: Base coat should never be put on natural nails
Rich cream makes the base coat set too fast
The cream under the polish stops it sticking
The cream turns the base coat cloudy when it dries
questions.why: Oil on the nail plate prevents polish from gripping, so it peels and lifts. After the massage, the nail plates are cleaned with remover.

questions.q: What was wrong with the 100-grit file?
o: It is too fine and will not shape the nail properly
It is too coarse for natural nails and can damage them
A file with a number should only be used on toenails
It leaves the nails too smooth, so polish slides off
questions.why: The lower the grit number, the coarser the file. Coarse files are for artificial nails; natural nails are filed with a fine grit, from the sides to the centre, in one direction.

questions.q: To neaten polish that got onto Shelly-Ann's skin, what should Amoy use?
o: Her thumbnail, once the polish has set
A fine brush or wrapped orange stick dipped in remover
A dry cotton bud, pressed on the skin
A cotton pad soaked in remover, wiped over the whole finger
questions.why: A fine brush or wrapped orange stick with a little remover lifts stray polish from the skin without touching the nail. A soaked pad takes the colour off the nail, and a thumbnail scratches.

questions.q: How should Kayla adapt the manicure for Delroy?
o: Refuse to treat him, because his nails are too short and bitten
Give a gentle manicure with a buffed finish and cuticle oil
Apply a clear coat of polish, as that is what 'nothing shiny' means
Nip the sore cuticles right back so that they heal faster
questions.why: He wants a neat, natural look, so the service is a gentle manicure with a buffed finish and cuticle oil in place of polish. Sore skin is softened, not cut.

questions.q: What should Kayla do about the small dry cut on his knuckle?
o: Avoid that area, and cover it if the Centre allows
Refuse to give him a manicure until it has healed
Clean it with remover and carry on over the cut
Massage over it firmly so that it heals faster
questions.why: A small cut restricts the service rather than stopping it. It is avoided in the massage and covered if needed, so germs cannot enter and the product does not sting.

questions.q: Which aftercare advice suits a mechanic who bites his nails?
o: Soak the hands in warm soapy water every night
Hand cream and cuticle oil daily, and gloves for work
Keep the nails very short, so there is nothing to bite
Wash the hands with a strong solvent to remove engine oil
questions.why: Moisturising cream and oil soften sore cuticles and reduce the urge to pick, and gloves protect the skin from oil and chemicals. Solvents and long soaks dry the skin.

questions.q: A client's fingernail has lifted away from the nail bed at the tip. The area under it looks yellow-white, with no pain or redness. What should you do?
o: Avoid pressing or filing under it; advise a doctor if it spreads
Push the lifted nail back down onto the bed with the orange stick
Clip away the lifted part and file the new edge smooth
Fill the gap under the nail with base coat to hold it down
questions.why: A lifting nail (onycholysis) is not pushed, clipped or glued: that traps germs and can hurt the nail bed. Keep the area clean and dry, work around it and advise a doctor if it spreads, hurts or changes colour.
